column4: God gives and removes dominion and gives honor and humiliation as He wills; visible authority and wealth therefore cannot decide who has truly been honored.
The same address says God provides whom He wills without account, placing provision under the One who has just been named as the giver of honor and humiliation.
When warning is forgotten, every gate is opened until the recipients rejoice in what they received, then seizure comes suddenly; abundance can be part of an adverse trial rather than approval.
God replaces hardship with ease until people prosper and dismiss both as ordinary history, then takes them unawares; alternating conditions test recognition rather than reveal rank.
The afflicted person calls God in every posture, then after relief passes on as if he never called; restored ease fails to produce remembered dependence.
When people taste mercy after adversity, they scheme against God's signs; the favorable turn is received as license rather than accountable care.
The patient people who do good are the stated exception to the despair and boastfulness of 11:9-10, showing the fitting response across both conditions.
Increase is tied to gratitude and severe consequence to ingratitude; the decisive issue in received favor is response, not possession.
Unequal provision is used to expose denial of God's نعمة, preventing the larger share from becoming an independent personal entitlement.
Spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision are named together as divine gifts, followed by the charge that people deny God's favor.
People recognize God's نعمة and then deny it, precisely the failure of memory that lets received care stop at the self.
A secure town receiving abundant provision from every place becomes ungrateful for God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; plenty and restriction form one moral trial.
After the town's reversal, recipients are commanded to eat God's lawful good provision and be grateful for His favor; gratitude is the proper reading of supply.
Earth's adornment is made a test of who acts best, directly classifying attractive worldly possession as examination material.
The wealthy man enters his garden while wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, turning a received estate into imagined permanence.
He doubts the Hour and assumes that even a return to his Lord would yield something better, carrying worldly advantage into a claim of divine rank.
His companion says the sight of the garden should have prompted recognition that power belongs to God, even when the speaker has fewer goods and children.
When loss comes, no social group can help the garden owner against God and he cannot help himself; the following and wealth once used as rank prove powerless.
The garden scene closes by assigning true protection to God and calling His reward and outcome better, replacing the owner's material scale.
Earlier peoples made the same self-attributing claim as the person in 39:49, and what they earned did not avail them.
The consequences of those people's deeds struck them, and the present wrongdoers are warned likewise; the gift-as-entitlement claim has a concrete end.
Some promise that if God gives from His فضل they will give charity and become righteous, making provision an expressly anticipated test of generosity.
When God actually gives them from His فضل, they become miserly and turn away; abundance reveals the failure to pass favor onward.
Their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts, showing that the failed prosperity-test transforms the recipient rather than certifying him.
Saba is told to eat from its Lord's provision and be grateful amid two flourishing gardens; an ample land is explicitly a scene of accountable favor.
When the people turn away, the flood replaces their productive gardens with bitter growth, reversing abundance without changing the identity of the Lord.
The reversal is identified as recompense for ingratitude, locating the judgment in response to favor rather than in the mere possession or loss of it.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, showing that the estate used to exclude the poor remains wholly exposed to divine action.
The garden becomes like a harvested field before the owners arrive; the object of their proprietary certainty is removed in a night.
The most balanced owner recalls having urged them to glorify God, identifying forgotten Lordship inside the failed garden test.
The owners finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, replacing possessive certainty with accountable recognition.
The person has not attempted the steep path, introducing care for the captive, orphan, and destitute as the difficult use of human capacity.
The question asks what can make the steep path known, marking the following acts as the demanding measure of worth.
Freeing a person from bondage begins the path, placing social release beside feeding an orphan under scarcity.
The famine feeding also reaches a destitute person in the dust, widening outward care beyond the related orphan of 90:15.
Denial of judgment introduces the repulsion of the orphan at 107:2, rooting failed care in a false account of responsibility.
The passage ends with people withholding even small ordinary assistance, extending orphan-neglect into a settled habit of stopping benefit.
Failure to urge the feeding of the poor is named among the causes of punishment, closely repeating the social omission next to the orphan in the section's surah.
The condemned admit that they did not feed the poor, making withheld nourishment a disclosed reason for their final abasement.
The command to race toward forgiveness and the garden leads directly to those who spend in ease and hardship at 3:134; generous action is the field of the race.
The warning not to admire wealth and children repeats 9:55, reinforcing that the same apparent favors can operate as punishment rather than honor.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor opened without limit; it locates honorable giving between miserliness and self-ruining excess before 17:30 names variable provision.
Those who spend must not follow their gift with reminders or injury; received help may not be turned into the kind of status debt Pharaoh asserts over Moses.
Charity is nullified by reminders, injury, display, and lack of faith, distinguishing genuine ikram from a giver's performance of superiority.
Charitable men and women who make a good loan receive multiplication and أجر كريم; noble reward is attached to outward generosity.
Moses' mother sends his sister to follow him from a distance, adding vigilant family concern to the exposed infant's foster-care scene.
After Moses refuses other wet nurses, his sister directs the household to a family that will nurture him sincerely; provision, nursing, and restored kinship converge.
Daughters and sons alike are described as gifts God grants as He wills, correcting the parent who treats a daughter as humiliation.
God combines sons and daughters or leaves whom He wills childless, placing every family configuration under gift and measure rather than social rank.
Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision are declared lost; child-destruction and the misreading of provision are joined in one judgment.
When Abraham's son reaches the age of working beside him, father and child face the dream together; a nurtured child becomes the center of a grave test, not a possession proving favor.
God explicitly calls the father-son ordeal the clear trial, bringing family love and divine testing into the same scene.
The son is ransomed with a great sacrifice, so the trial ends in preserved life rather than treating the child as expendable property.
Abraham is tested with commands and fulfills them before being made a leader, so rank follows faithful response to trial rather than material reception.
Worldly life is beautified for disbelievers who mock believers, yet the people of taqwa are above them at resurrection and God provides without account.
Children, accumulated gold and silver, livestock, and cultivated land are listed as beautified desires and then called only the provision of worldly life.
The next ayah offers enduring gardens and God's approval as better than the status objects of 3:14, separating true favor from near adornment.
Disbelievers point to the two parties' comparative station and assembly, using visible social setting as an argument against revelation.
God recalls generations with better furnishings and appearance whom He destroyed, refuting the claim that impressive worldly station signals worth.
The Merciful may extend the straying person's condition until the promised consequence reveals who truly has the worse station and weaker support.
A disbeliever confidently claims that he will be given wealth and children, converting hoped-for provision into proof of continuing privilege.
God will inherit what the claimant speaks of and he will come alone, stripping wealth and children from the status claim.
People love the immediate life, naming the preference that turns present provision into the dominant scale.
They leave the hereafter behind, identifying what the near-life preference excludes from their judgment.
People prefer the worldly life, a concise diagnosis of why its expansion can be mistaken for honor.
The hereafter is better and more lasting, supplying the scale omitted by that preference.
Rivalry in abundance distracts people, directly portraying possessions and numbers as a competition for rank.
The distraction lasts until the graves, giving the abundance-rivalry its terminal boundary before questioning about نعيم.
The Prophet frowns and turns away, beginning a correction of attention distributed by perceived social standing.
The person from whom he turns is blind and has actively come for guidance, marking the overlooked party as vulnerable yet seeking benefit.
The self-sufficient man receives the privileged attention, echoing the false rank attached to perceived independence.
The Prophet attends closely to that self-sufficient person, making status-based allocation of care visible as an action.
The other man comes striving, supplying the moral quality hidden by his low social visibility.
The striving, fearful man is neglected, a direct social reversal of honoring the person most in need of reception.
Noah's elite dismiss his followers as the lowest people and judge them by superficial opinion, illustrating human rank inferred from visible condition.
Noah refuses to drive believers away and says their account is with their Lord; elite preference cannot dictate who receives the messenger's care.
Noah will not say that God grants no good to those whom elite eyes despise; visible poverty cannot establish divine humiliation.
Noah's people object that the lowest people follow him, making social inferiority their reason to reject truth.
Noah refuses to expel the believers, preserving vulnerable followers against the powerful audience's status demand.
The well-provided town also receives a messenger from among itself and rejects him; its later deprivation follows failed response to both provision and guidance.
Givers must spend from good things they earned and not choose inferior goods they themselves would accept only reluctantly; the recipient must be treated with honor.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily, giving a measured form to responsible use of provision.
Those who are miserly and command miserliness are reminded that God is self-sufficient; retained wealth supplies no independence from Him.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, presenting released wealth as the route through which provision yields good.
God raises believers and people of knowledge in degrees, locating genuine elevation in faith and knowledge rather than possessions.
Those who seek honor with disbelieving allies are asked whether they do not know that all honor belongs to God.
The Prophet is consoled that all honor belongs to God, setting a firm boundary against human assignment of worth.
Adopted sons are not made biological sons merely by declaration, supplying a legal boundary around household care and claimed parenthood.
Adopted children should be called by their fathers when known and otherwise treated as brothers and clients, preserving belonging without falsifying lineage.
The human is created from a mixed drop in order to be tested and is equipped with hearing and sight; nurture and trial begin together at human origin.
The generous Lord of 82:6 is the One who created, proportioned, and balanced the person, making His generosity formative care rather than material indulgence alone.
God composes the human in whatever form He wills, completing the picture of measured Lordly formation.
The giver affirms the best promise, distinguishing his inward reading of provision from the miser's denial.
God eases the giver toward ease, continuing the outcome attached to generosity rather than hoarded abundance.
The self-sufficient miser denies the best promise, stating the inner counterpart of his withholding.
He is eased toward hardship, reversing his assumption that retained wealth secures ease.
Ease is promised with hardship, discouraging the restricted person from reading difficulty as abandonment.
The repeated promise that ease accompanies hardship reinforces that constriction is not a final verdict of humiliation.
Abraham promptly brings a roasted calf to the messengers who arrive with good news, another concrete Quranic scene in which receiving guests means feeding them.
Lot identifies the visitors as his guests and asks his people not to disgrace him through their treatment, making a host responsible for another's protected standing.
The command not to shame the guests places honor at the boundary between sheltering a vulnerable visitor and exposing him to abuse.
